newsitem.title: USA: Winter wheat sowings plunge, U.S. supply seen tight.
newsitem.headline: Winter wheat sowings plunge, U.S. supply seen tight.

text.p: American farmers sowed only 48.2 million acres of winter wheat, the smallest total since 1978, suggesting a scanty wheat stockpile for at least another year, the Agriculture Department said Friday.

It forecast 374 million bushels of wheat would be on hand -- well below normal -- when the new crop was ready for harvest this summer. Some 1.22 billion bushels were in U.S. grain bins and warehouses on Dec. 1, about what analysts expected, but the smallest figure for that time of the year since 1987.

Wheat supplies and sowings are crucial figures, private analyst John Schnittker said, because of a two-year run of tight supplies and high prices. Winter wheat, which is planted in the fall and harvested the following summer, provides the lion's share of the U.S. wheat supply, so small acreage could presage a small harvest.
Analysts had expected 51.4 million acres would be sown to winter wheat for 1997.
Instead, farmers planted 48.2 million acres of winter wheat for this year's harvest, 7 percent less than the 52 million acres sown for the 1996 crop.

This season's crop will be the first under the "Freedom to Farm" law, which removed most federal controls on farming and gave farmers the chance to pursue attractive prices. However, dry weather discouraged early seeding in the Great Plains, and a rainy fall prevented planting in the Midwest and in Kansas, the No. 1 wheat state.

The Agriculture Department forecast 155 million bushels of soybeans and 959 million bushels of corn would be on hand when the new crop matures -- both down from one month ago. Some 1.82 billion bushels of soybeans and 6.91 billion bushels of corn were in bins on Dec. 1, slightly lower than analysts expected.

In its final look at 1996 crop output, the department put the corn crop at 9.293 billion bushels. It lowered its estimate of soybeans marginally to 2.382 billion bushels and kept wheat at 2.281 billion bushels.
The corn crop was the third-largest ever and soybeans the second-largest, but both would barely satisfy a voracious appetite at home and abroad for U.S. grains and oilseeds.
